semantic_correction.stem: A nurse on a perinatal quality-improvement team is reviewing racial and ethnic inequities in maternal outcomes. Which proposed approach best addresses factors that can contribute to those inequities?

options.A: Review care processes with access and language barriers, social and structural determinants, referral needs, and potential stereotyping or bias when planning QI.
options.B: Center the review on patient education and self-management choices, adding health-system or access factors when individual adherence appears inadequate.
options.C: Compare whether each group received the same written materials and appointment schedule, using equal distribution as evidence that access and care were equivalent.
options.D: Limit the review to obstetric diagnoses and treatment complications, separating transportation, interpreter needs, and other social factors from clinical QI.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC's current HEAR HER guidance for obstetric professionals recommends inquiring about and documenting social and structural determinants that may influence health and use of health care, maximizing referrals to social services, providing interpreter access when clinician and patient languages differ, recognizing that stereotyping can harm patient interactions, and avoiding attribution of patient behavior solely to individual choices without recognizing social and structural factors. CDC also emphasizes respectful, patient-centered care and attention to implicit bias as components of addressing disparities. The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan places performance/quality improvement, unbiased treatment and equal access, multidisciplinary collaboration, referral assessment, and evidence-based resource use within Management of Care. Therefore A is the best QI approach because it examines health-system care processes together with the access, communication, structural, referral, and bias-related factors that can affect care. B overweights individual behavior. C confuses equal distribution of materials with equivalent access and quality. D excludes factors CDC specifically identifies as relevant to patient health and use of care.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: When reviewing inequities in maternal outcomes, evaluate care processes together with access and communication barriers, social and structural determinants, referral needs, and potential stereotyping or bias rather than attributing outcomes primarily to individual patient behavior.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_version_date: CDC page dated May 15, 2024; current live page rechecked August 20, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Address Health Inequities: inquire about and document social and structural determinants of health that may influence health and use of health care; maximize referrals to social services; provide interpreter access when patient and clinician languages differ; recognize harmful stereotyping; avoid solely attributing patient behaviors to individual choices without recognizing social and structural factors; provide respectful patient-centered care and address implicit biases.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Maternal-health equity work should account for social and structural determinants, access and language needs, referrals, stereotyping, and bias rather than reducing patient behavior or care outcomes to individual choices alone.
semantic_correction.blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7 (official PDF pageno 10): participate in performance improvement projects and quality improvement processes; identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members; provide unbiased treatment and equal access to care; assess the need for referrals and obtain necessary orders; utilize resources to promote quality client care, including evidence-based research and policies/procedures.
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — equity-focused perinatal quality improvement and access to care
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the maternal-equity quality-improvement construct, removed the uniquely-long correct-answer pattern, rebuilt A/B/C/D as comparable QI strategies, and grounded the key directly in current CDC HEAR HER recommendations plus the NCSBN 2026 Management of Care quality-improvement and equal-access framework.

scope_exclusions.causal_attribution: The item does not claim that any one structural, social, access, or bias factor explains a specific individual outcome; it tests the breadth of a systems-level quality-improvement review.
scope_exclusions.racial_essentialism: Race or ethnicity is not treated as a biologic cause of outcome differences; the review focuses on care processes and potentially modifiable access, communication, social, structural, and bias-related factors.
scope_exclusions.individual_behavior: Patient education and self-management remain relevant, but they should not be reviewed in isolation from health-system and social or structural context.
scope_exclusions.equal_vs_equitable: Providing identical written materials does not by itself demonstrate equivalent communication, access, comprehension, or quality of care.
scope_exclusions.interpreter_services: The item does not test a particular interpreter vendor or legal reimbursement rule; it uses CDC's recommendation to provide interpreter access when patient and clinician languages differ.
scope_exclusions.specific_intervention: The item asks how to frame a QI review rather than prescribing one intervention or assuming that every identified barrier has the same remedy.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for ‘perinatal quality improvement maternal inequities social structural determinants interpreter stereotyping bias access’ returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank scan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It combines systems-level care review with the access, language, SDOH, referral, stereotyping, and bias factors directly identified by CDC.
option_audit.B: Plausible because patient education and self-management matter, but CDC explicitly cautions against reducing behavior to individual choices without social and structural context.
option_audit.C: Plausible because standardization can reduce unwarranted variation, but equal distribution of the same materials does not establish equivalent access, communication, or care quality.
option_audit.D: Plausible because diagnoses and treatment complications belong in clinical QI, but excluding transportation, interpreter needs, and related social/access factors creates an incomplete equity review.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A is the only option that deliberately combines clinical care processes with CDC-identified access, communication, structural, referral, and bias factors. B individualizes the problem, C mistakes sameness for equivalent access, and D excludes relevant contextual factors.

cueing_check.note: The key is not longest; all alternatives are parallel quality-improvement approaches of comparable length and none relies on all/only/always/never/every cueing.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN Management of Care explicitly includes quality improvement, unbiased treatment/equal access, multidisciplinary collaboration, referrals, and evidence-based resource use, directly supporting an entry-level RN role on a perinatal QI team.
